introduction-kubernetes-is-an-operating-.core: Kubernetes is like an operating system for the datacentre: powerful, general-purpose and complex. Platform teams decide how much of it to expose to developers, from thin wrappers (raw Kubernetes with guardrails) to thick wrappers (PaaS-like abstractions).

first_principles.problem: Developers face hundreds of Kubernetes concepts just to deploy a web app, or are hidden from the details they need for debugging.
truths: Most apps need a small subset.
Every abstraction trades power for simplicity.

analogy.title: A professional industrial kitchen
analogy.story: It has every tool imaginable, but a home cook needs a simpler station, or a guide to the right tools.
analogy.breaks: Exposure can vary per team: the same platform can offer both.

example.title: Two developer experiences
flow: Thin: write Deployment/Service YAML with policy checks
Thick: `platform deploy --image x` and nothing else

steps.label: Insight
steps.detail: The same infrastructure, very different interfaces.

check.q: Why is Kubernetes compared to an operating system?
check.a: It's a powerful, general-purpose platform for running workloads, with far more capability and complexity than most applications need directly.

the-thin-wrapper-kubernetes-native.core: Thin wrappers expose the Kubernetes API directly with guardrails (policies, templates, Helm charts, namespaces with RBAC). This maximises flexibility, keeps standard tooling and skills transferable, but demands more Kubernetes knowledge from developers.

first_principles.problem: Expert teams are frustrated by a PaaS that hides features they need (sidecars, custom probes, CRDs).
derivation: Support standard **kubectl, Helm and GitOps** tooling.

analogy.title: 'Here are the keys, drive safely'
analogy.story: You get the real car with a few safety features enforced, not a simplified go-kart.
analogy.breaks: It carries a high cognitive load for teams without Kubernetes expertise.

check.q: What's the main trade-off of a thin wrapper?
check.a: Maximum flexibility and standard tooling at the cost of higher Kubernetes knowledge requirements for developers.

the-thick-wrapper-platform-as-a-service.core: Thick wrappers hide Kubernetes behind a custom PaaS-like abstraction (a CLI, a simple spec, Heroku-style 'give me your code'). They minimise cognitive load and enforce consistency, but the platform team owns a custom product and its limits.

first_principles.problem: Product developers without Kubernetes skills get lost in YAML and make insecure configurations.
truths: Most apps fit a few patterns.
derivation: **Maintain** it as a product (docs, versions, support).

analogy.title: 'Just give me your code'
analogy.story: A valet service: hand over the keys and the car is parked, no driving required.
analogy.breaks: Hidden complexity resurfaces at the edges (debugging, unusual needs).

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Deploy in one line, compliant by default.

code.text:
platform deploy --app orders --image ghcr.io/acme/orders:1.2 --public
# platform generates Deployment, Service, Ingress, HPA, PDB, NetworkPolicy

check.q: What's the main cost of a thick wrapper for the platform team?
check.a: Building and maintaining a custom abstraction product that must handle edge cases and evolve with needs.

the-leaky-abstraction-why-thick-wrappers.core: Every abstraction has a ceiling. Thick wrappers break down when apps need features the wrapper doesn't model (custom probes, sidecars, stateful sets) or when failures surface as underlying Kubernetes errors developers were never taught to read.

first_principles.problem: A team hits a wrapper limitation, can't escape it, and either waits months for a platform feature or bypasses the platform entirely.
truths: No escape hatch means shadow IT.
derivation: **Track** requests for unsupported features and evolve.

analogy.title: A pre-set microwave with no manual mode
analogy.story: Fine for popcorn, useless for anything the presets don't cover.
analogy.breaks: Too many escape hatches turn a thick wrapper back into a thin one.

example.title: Hitting the ceiling
flow: No escape → team deploys outside platform
Fix: add an overlay escape hatch + roadmap item

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: The team stays on the platform.

example.outcome: thick wrappers designed with their limits in mind.

check.q: What typically happens when a thick wrapper has no escape hatch?
check.a: Teams with unsupported needs bypass the platform, creating shadow IT.

choosing-your-strategy-the-decision-matr.core: The right wrapper thickness depends on workload diversity, developer Kubernetes skill, compliance needs and platform team capacity. Many organisations use a layered approach: a thick golden path for common apps and thin access for experts.

first_principles.problem: Teams argue thick vs thin in absolute terms instead of fitting the choice to their context.
derivation: **Layered**: thick paved road + thin escape lane.

analogy.title: Choosing between a bus service and car hire
analogy.story: Most commuters take the bus (simple, fixed routes); some need a hire car for unusual trips.
analogy.breaks: Layering adds maintenance of two paths, so keep both well-supported.

example.title: Applying the matrix
flow: Org A: 200 similar web apps, few K8s experts → thick
Org B: ML, data, streaming, strong SREs → thin + templates

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Each org gets the wrapper it needs.

check.q: When is a thick wrapper most appropriate?
check.a: When workloads are fairly uniform and most developers lack deep Kubernetes expertise.
